items.title: Overview
items.text:
BetterPy uses CalVer (Calendar Versioning) with the format: YYYY.MM.PATCH[-channel.build] (MM is zero-padded)

This versioning scheme provides: - Clear timeline visibility for releases - Natural alignment with monthly release cadence - Support for multiple release channels (stable, beta, dev) - Simple bugfix tracking

items.title: Base Format: YYYY.MM.PATCH
items.text:
• YYYY: 4-digit year
  • MM: Month without leading zero (1-12)
  • PATCH: Bugfix/patch number (starts at 0)

items.title: Channel Suffix: -channel.build
items.text: Optional suffix for pre-release and development builds: - channel: Release channel name (dev, beta, alpha, rc) - build: Build number or timestamp

items.title: Stable Releases
items.text:
Monthly production releases following calendar months.

Format: YYYY.MM.0

Examples: - 2026.01.0 - January 2026 release - 2026.02.0 - February 2026 release - 2026.12.0 - December 2026 release

When to use: - Regular monthly feature releases - Production-ready code - Published to default channel in JetBrains Marketplace

items.title: Bugfix Releases
items.text:
Patch releases for urgent fixes within a monthly cycle.

Format: YYYY.MM.PATCH (where PATCH > 0)

Examples: - 2026.01.1 - First bugfix for January 2026 - 2026.01.2 - Second bugfix for January 2026

When to use: - Critical bug fixes - Security patches - Hot fixes between monthly releases

items.title: Development Builds
items.text:
Unstable development snapshots with timestamps.

Format: YYYY.MM.0-dev.YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS

Examples: - 2026.01.0-dev.20260115-143000 - 2026.02.0-dev.20260203-091500

When to use: - Automated CI builds - Feature branch testing - Internal development testing - Published to dev channel

items.title: Beta Releases
items.text:
Pre-release versions for wider testing before stable release.

Format: YYYY.MM.0-beta.N

Examples: - 2026.01.0-beta.1 - First beta - 2026.01.0-beta.2 - Second beta

When to use: - Feature complete but needs testing - User acceptance testing - Published to beta channel

items.title: Alpha Releases
items.text:
Early pre-release versions for initial testing.

Format: YYYY.MM.0-alpha.N

Examples: - 2026.01.0-alpha.1 - 2026.01.0-alpha.2

When to use: - Early feature testing - Breaking changes testing - Published to alpha channel

items.title: Release Candidates
items.text:
Final testing before stable release.

Format: YYYY.MM.0-rc.N

Examples: - 2026.01.0-rc.1 - 2026.01.0-rc.2

When to use: - Final testing phase - No new features, only bug fixes - Published to rc channel

items.title: IntelliJ Marketplace Channels
items.text:
The build system automatically routes versions to appropriate channels:

Version Pattern Channel Visibility 2026.01.0 default All users 2026.01.1 default All users 2026.01.0-beta.X beta Beta testers 2026.01.0-alpha.X alpha Alpha testers 2026.01.0-rc.X rc RC testers 2026.01.0-dev.X dev Developers only

items.title: Version Management Script
items.text: Use scripts/version.sh for automated version management:

items.title: Show Current Version
items.text: ./scripts/version.sh current

items.title: Preview Next Version
items.text:
# Next stable monthly release
./scripts/version.sh next --channel=stable

# Next bugfix
./scripts/version.sh next --channel=bugfix

# Next dev build
./scripts/version.sh next --channel=dev

# Next beta
./scripts/version.sh next --channel=beta

items.title: Bump Version
items.text:
# Bump to next stable release
./scripts/version.sh bump --channel=stable

# Bump to next bugfix
./scripts/version.sh bump --channel=bugfix

# Create dev build
./scripts/version.sh bump --channel=dev

# Create beta release
./scripts/version.sh bump --channel=beta

The script automatically: - Updates gradle.properties - Creates a backup (.bak file) - Uses current date for stable/dev versions - Increments build numbers for beta/alpha/rc

items.title: Migration from SemVer
items.text:
If migrating from SemVer (e.g., 0.0.1):

  1. Choose appropriate CalVer version based on current date
  2. Update gradle.properties
  3. Update CHANGELOG.md with new section
  4. Tag the transition commit

Example: 

# New: 2026.01.0 (January 2026)
./scripts/version.sh bump --channel=stable

items.title: Best Practices
items.text:
1. Monthly Cadence: Aim for stable releases at the start of each month
  2. Bugfix Windows: Reserve patches for critical fixes only
  3. Beta Testing: Use beta channel for 1-2 weeks before stable
  4. Dev Builds: Automate in CI for every commit to main
  5. Changelog: Always update CHANGELOG.md before tagging
  6. Testing: Test beta/rc thoroughly before promoting to stable
  7. Communication: Announce releases with clear channel information

items.title: FAQ
items.text:
Q: What if I need to release twice in one month? A: Use patch versions (e.g., 2026.01.0, then 2026.01.1 if needed)

Q: Can I skip months? A: Yes! If no release in February, go directly to 2026.03.0 in March

Q: How do I handle multiple features in development? A: Use dev builds (-dev.timestamp) or feature branches with beta releases

Q: What about breaking changes? A: Document in CHANGELOG.md and consider using beta cycle for user feedback

Q: Can I use week numbers instead of months? A: Yes, modify the script to use YYYY.WW.PATCH format (week of year)

items.title: Documentation Development
items.text: This project uses Zensical with the Material for MkDocs theme to manage its documentation.

items.title: Local Setup
items.text:
To serve and preview the documentation locally, you'll need uv installed.

  1. Serve the documentation (with live-rendered placeholders): 

    uv run docs serve
    (Fallback: uv run python scripts/build_docs.py serve.)

    This wraps zensical serve and starts a local preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000/. The page reloads when you edit anything under docs/ or any feature metadata block under src/main/resources/META-INF/features/*.xml.

    Do not run uv run zensical serve directly

    Our docs use placeholders such as 11, 6, and <!-- feature: <id> --> blocks that are expanded from feature metadata at render time. A plain zensical serve does not invoke that rendering pipeline, so the live preview will show the raw placeholders rather than the production output. Always use the docs serve wrapper.

  2. Build the site once: 

    uv run docs build
    Produces site/, matching what the release pipeline builds.

  3. Add a new dependency: 

    uv add <package-name>

items.title: How the docs build works
items.text: The committed files under docs/ are the single source of truth and are never mutated by any build or serve command. Both docs build and docs serve first render every docs/**/*.md file into a shadow directory at build/docs-rendered-root/docs/ (git-ignored), expanding placeholders and feature blocks, then run zensical against that shadow tree. The committed zensical.toml is likewise copied (nav-trimmed for empty groups) rather than rewritten in place. See scripts/build_docs.py and scripts/docs_ext.py in the repo for details.

items.title: Recovery
items.text:
If git status shows unexpected changes under docs/ — typically left over from an interrupted run of the legacy pre-refactor script — restore them with:

git checkout -- docs/

The current pipeline never writes into docs/, so such leftovers can only come from an older version of the build script or from manual edits.

items.title: Project Structure
items.text:
• zensical.toml: Configuration file for the documentation (theme, navigation, extensions).
  • docs/: Directory containing the Markdown source files for the documentation.
  • docs/index.md: The home page of the documentation.

items.title: Updating Marketplace Screenshots (UI Tests)
items.text:
The documentation and marketplace page rely on automated screenshots generated by UI tests. Since these tests require a running IDE instance via the Robot Server plugin, they are excluded from the standard ./gradlew test task.

To regenerate these screenshots locally:

  1. Start the IDE with the Robot Server: 

    ./gradlew runIdeForUiTests
    Wait for the PyCharm IDE to fully start.

  2. Run the screenshot test class in a separate terminal: 

    ./gradlew test --tests "*PluginPageScreenshotsTest*"

The new screenshots will be saved automatically to docs/assets/marketplace/ and can be committed.

items.title: Feature layout
items.text: This document explains how features are organized in the BetterPy plugin and how to add a new one.

items.title: Files per feature
items.text:
Each feature consists of XML fragment files only:

  • Canonical feature file: src/main/resources/META-INF/features/<id>.xml — holds plugin registrations and the feature metadata in a dedicated XML comment block.
  • Optional sibling registration files: src/main/resources/META-INF/features/<id>[.<suffix>].xml — additional registrations split by optional dependency or registration type.

Metadata block format inside canonical XML files:

<!-- betterpy-feature
id: add-self-parameter
displayName: Add self parameter
description: Adds a missing self parameter to instance methods
category: CODE_STRUCTURE
maturity: STABLE
defaultEnabled: true
-->

Rules: - Metadata is parsed only from canonical <id>.xml files (not from suffixed siblings). - The metadata id must match the canonical filename <id>.xml.

A feature's canonical <id>.xml holds its <extensions>, <actions>, <group>, <extensionPoints>, and <projectListeners> registrations in one place. Sibling files exist only for optional-dependency wiring (.mcp.xml, .yamlsupport.xml, .structuralsearch.xml) and for the Pythonid extension namespace (.pythonid.xml).

At build time, GeneratePluginXmlFragmentsTask globs the committed per-feature XML files, filters them by the active release channel, and emits 4 aggregator files (xi:include indexes). plugin.xml xi:includes the aggregators; the aggregators xi:include the per-feature files. plugin.xml itself only contains plugin metadata, <depends> entries, <resource-bundle>, and the xi:include seam — no <extensions>, <actions>, <group>, or <extensionPoints> live there.

items.title: Filename suffix → aggregator routing
items.text:
The suffix on a per-feature XML filename decides which aggregator references it:

Filename Aggregator Purpose <id>.xml META-INF/plugin-features-index.xml Default target: <extensions> (com.intellij namespace), <actions>, <group>, <extensionPoints>, <projectListeners> <id>.pythonid.xml META-INF/plugin-features-index.xml Pythonid namespace (PythonCore extension points) <id>.mcp.xml META-INF/mcp-support.xml MCP optional dependency (com.intellij.mcpServer) <id>.yamlsupport.xml META-INF/yaml-support.xml YAML optional dependency <id>.structuralsearch.xml META-INF/structural-search.xml Structural Search optional dependency

Each per-feature XML file must declare its own <extensions defaultExtensionNs="…">; the suffix only decides which aggregator xi:includes it, not the namespace wrapping.

items.title: Channel filter
items.text:
src/main/resources/feature-sets/dev.yaml and stable.yaml list the feature ids included in each release channel. Building with -PreleaseChannel=stable (or RELEASE_CHANNEL=stable) filters aggregator entries to the stable list; dev (the default) includes everything.

A feature that is absent from the active channel's set has no xi:include entry in the aggregators, so its extensions are not registered with the platform. The XML file itself is still copied into the build output but nothing loads it.

items.title: The _bootstrap special case
items.text:
src/main/resources/META-INF/features/_bootstrap.xml holds non-user-facing registrations (errorHandler, PluginSettingsState, bootstrap file-based indexes, application configurables, the pytestFixtureProvider extension point, cross-feature action groups like MyPlugin.CopySpecialGroup / PytestExplorerPopupMenu, EmptyAction placeholders, and dev/internal actions). Unlike every other feature, _bootstrap is always emitted regardless of the active channel.

_bootstrap is the only allowed _-prefixed feature id. The generator throws a GradleException if any other feature id starts with _.

items.title: Workflow: adding a new feature
items.text:
1. Create src/main/resources/META-INF/features/<id>.xml and add a <!-- betterpy-feature ... --> metadata block.
  2. Add <idea-plugin><extensions …>…</extensions></idea-plugin> registrations in that canonical file, and create any suffixed variants for optional dependencies / Pythonid registrations.
  3. If the feature should ship in the stable channel, add its id to src/main/resources/feature-sets/stable.yaml.
  4. Run the feature-flag tests to confirm nothing drifted: 
    ./gradlew test --tests com.github.chbndrhnns.betterpy.featureflags.*

No regeneration task is needed — the per-feature XML files are authoritative, and the aggregators are rebuilt automatically during processResources.

items.title: Current state
items.text: Feature declaration metadata is XML-only. Canonical META-INF/features/<id>.xml files are the sole source of feature metadata used by runtime loading, defaults/registry wiring, and build-time plugin XML aggregation.

items.title: Generating Feature Documentation
items.text: The FeatureDocumentationGenerator generates documentation for all plugin features from their YAML feature declarations. This is useful for maintaining up-to-date feature references and for external tooling.

items.title: Overview
items.text:
The generator is located at: 

src/main/kotlin/com/github/chbndrhnns/intellijplatformplugincopy/settings/FeatureDocumentationGenerator.kt

It provides three output formats:

Method Description Output generateMarkdown() Full documentation with tables, badges, and YouTrack links Markdown generateJson() Machine-readable feature data JSON generateSimpleList() Quick reference list with status indicators Plain text

All methods accept an optional includeHidden: Boolean = false parameter to include hidden features.

items.title: Running the Generator
items.text: Since FeatureDocumentationGenerator uses FeatureRegistry.instance(), it requires the IntelliJ Platform application context. There are several ways to run it:

items.title: Option 1: Gradle Task (Recommended)
items.text:
The easiest way to generate documentation is using the dedicated Gradle task:

./gradlew generateFeatureDocs

This will generate:

  • docs/features/feature-reference.md - Full markdown documentation
  • docs/features/features.json - Machine-readable JSON format

The task runs the GenerateFeatureDocsTest which is excluded from the normal test suite.

Excluded from normal tests

The GenerateFeatureDocsTest is automatically excluded when running ./gradlew test. It only runs when explicitly invoked via generateFeatureDocs or with the -PrunDocGenTest=true flag.

items.title: Option 2: Direct Test Invocation
items.text:
You can also run the test directly with the property flag:

./gradlew test --tests "*.GenerateFeatureDocsTest" -PrunDocGenTest=true

Or run a specific test method:

./gradlew test --tests "*.GenerateFeatureDocsTest.testGenerateMarkdownDocs" -PrunDocGenTest=true

items.title: Option 3: From the IDE Plugin (Runtime)
items.text:
You can invoke the generator from within the running plugin, for example via an action:

class GenerateFeatureDocsAction : AnAction("Generate Feature Docs") {
    override fun actionPerformed(e: AnActionEvent) {
        val markdown = FeatureDocumentationGenerator.generateMarkdown()

        // Copy to clipboard
        CopyPasteManager.getInstance().setContents(StringSelection(markdown))

        // Or show in a dialog
        Messages.showInfoMessage(e.project, "Documentation generated and copied to clipboard", "Feature Docs")
    }
}

items.title: Option 4: From runIde Task
items.text:
1. Start the plugin in development mode: 

    ./gradlew runIde

  2. Open the Kotlin scratch file or use Evaluate Expression in the debugger: 

    com.github.chbndrhnns.betterpy.featureflags.FeatureDocumentationGenerator.generateMarkdown()

items.title: Integrating with CI/CD
items.text:
To automatically generate and commit documentation on release:

# .github/workflows/docs.yml
- name: Generate feature docs
  run: ./gradlew generateFeatureDocs

- name: Commit docs
  run: |
    git add docs/features/feature-reference.md docs/features/features.json
    git commit -m "docs: update feature reference" || true

items.title: Adding Feature Metadata
items.text:
To ensure your features appear in the generated documentation, add a YAML declaration under src/main/resources/features and bind the toggle to the same ID:

@Feature("my-feature")
var enableMyFeature: Boolean = FeatureDefaults.defaultEnabled("my-feature")

See FeatureMetadata.kt for the binding annotation definition.

items.title: Marketplace Release Management
items.text: This guide covers how to manage BetterPy releases on the JetBrains Marketplace using the Marketplace REST API.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
• A Marketplace API token (permanent token). Generate one at: https://plugins.jetbrains.com/author/me/tokens
  • The plugin numeric ID. BetterPy's ID is 29896.

Tip: You can look up the numeric ID from the XML plugin ID: 

curl -s "https://plugins.jetbrains.com/api/plugins?family=intellij&xmlId=com.github.chbndrhnns.betterpy" \
  | python3 -m json.tool | grep '"id"'

items.title: Common Operations
items.text:
All examples below use the environment variable $MP_TOKEN for the API token:

export MP_TOKEN="perm:your-token-here"

items.title: List All Published Versions
items.text:
curl -s \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MP_TOKEN" \
  "https://plugins.jetbrains.com/api/plugins/29896/updates" \
  | python3 -c "
import json, sys
for u in json.load(sys.stdin):
    ch = u.get('channel') or '(stable)'
    print(f\"id={u['id']}  version={u['version']}  channel={ch}\")
"

Each update has a numeric id (the update ID) which is needed for deletion.

items.title: Delete a Specific Version
items.text:
Use the update ID (not the version string) to delete a release:

curl -s -w "\nHTTP %{http_code}\n" \
  -X DELETE \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MP_TOKEN" \
  "https://plugins.jetbrains.com/api/updates/{updateId}"

Replace {updateId} with the numeric ID from the list command above.

A successful deletion returns HTTP 200 and the message "Update has been removed".

items.title: Delete Multiple Versions
items.text:
To delete several versions at once, first list them to get the update IDs, then loop:

for id in 1234 1235 1236; do
  echo "Deleting update $id..."
  curl -s -w " HTTP_CODE:%{http_code}\n" \
    -X DELETE \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $MP_TOKEN" \
    "https://plugins.jetbrains.com/api/updates/$id"
done

items.title: Upload a New Version
items.text:
Upload to the Stable channel (omit the channel field):

curl -i \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MP_TOKEN" \
  -F "pluginId=29896" \
  -F "file=@/path/to/plugin.zip" \
  "https://plugins.jetbrains.com/plugin/uploadPlugin"

Upload to a pre-release channel (beta, alpha, dev, etc.):

curl -i \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MP_TOKEN" \
  -F "pluginId=29896" \
  -F "file=@/path/to/plugin.zip" \
  -F "channel=beta" \
  "https://plugins.jetbrains.com/plugin/uploadPlugin"

Important — channel=default is NOT Stable. On the JetBrains Marketplace, the Stable channel is represented by an empty channel value. To publish to Stable, omit the channel form field entirely (or pass an empty string). Passing channel=default creates/uses a custom channel literally named default, which is separate from Stable and will not be shown as the default download.

You can verify via the list endpoint: Stable updates return an empty channel field (""), while custom channels return their literal name.

See VERSIONING.md for channel conventions.

items.title: API Endpoints Reference
items.text:
Operation Method Endpoint Plugin info (by XML ID) GET /api/plugins?family=intellij&xmlId={xmlId} List updates GET /api/plugins/{pluginId}/updates Delete an update DELETE /api/updates/{updateId} Upload plugin POST /plugin/uploadPlugin

Base URL: https://plugins.jetbrains.com

items.title: Important Notes
items.text:
• Deletion is permanent. There is no undo. Always verify the update IDs before deleting.
  • Authentication: All mutating operations require the Authorization: Bearer header with a valid permanent token.
  • Rate limiting: The Marketplace API may rate-limit requests. Add a short delay between bulk operations if needed.
  • The upload endpoint is documented in detail at: Plugin Upload API

items.title: MCP Server Context Passing Guide
items.text: This document explains how to pass and access context (project, editor, caret position) in MCP tools and how to implement navigation.

items.title: Overview
items.text: The MCP (Model Context Protocol) server in IntelliJ Platform provides tools that can interact with the IDE. Context is passed through: 1. Automatic context via CoroutineContext 2. Explicit parameters in tool methods

items.title: Accessing the Project
items.text:
The project is the primary context automatically available to MCP tools:

import com.intellij.mcpserver.project
import kotlinx.coroutines.currentCoroutineContext

suspend fun my_tool() {
    val project = currentCoroutineContext().project
    // Use project...
}

items.title: Project Context Details
items.text:
• Extension: CoroutineContext.project (throws if no project)
  • Extension: CoroutineContext.projectOrNull (returns null if no project)
  • Source: Defined in McpCallInfo.kt

The project can be specified by: - Environment variables - HTTP headers - Implicit tool parameter projectPath - If only one project is open, it's used automatically

items.title: Example from RefactoringToolset
items.text:
suspend fun rename_refactoring(
    pathInProject: String,
    symbolName: String,
    newName: String,
): String {
    val project = currentCoroutineContext().project
    val resolvedPath = project.resolveInProject(pathInProject)
    // ... rest of implementation
}

items.title: No Automatic Editor Context
items.text: Important: MCP tools do NOT receive automatic editor or caret context. The current editor state is not passed automatically.

items.title: Accessing Open Editors
items.text:
To work with editors, use FileEditorManagerEx:

import com.intellij.openapi.fileEditor.ex.FileEditorManagerEx

suspend fun get_open_editors() {
    val project = currentCoroutineContext().project
    val fileEditorManager = FileEditorManagerEx.getInstanceExAsync(project)

    // Get all open files
    val openFiles = fileEditorManager.openFiles

    // Get active editor
    val activeEditor = fileEditorManager.selectedEditor
    val activeFile = activeEditor?.file
}

items.title: Example from FileToolset
items.text:
@McpTool
suspend fun get_all_open_file_paths(): OpenFilesInfo {
    val project = currentCoroutineContext().project
    val projectDir = project.projectDirectory

    val fileEditorManager = FileEditorManagerEx.getInstanceExAsync(project)
    val openFiles = fileEditorManager.openFiles
    val filePaths = openFiles.mapNotNull { projectDir.relativizeIfPossible(it) }
    val activeFilePath = fileEditorManager.selectedEditor?.file?.toNioPathOrNull()
        ?.let { projectDir.relativize(it).pathString }

    return OpenFilesInfo(activeFilePath = activeFilePath, openFiles = filePaths)
}

items.title: Design Pattern: Explicit Parameters
items.text:
Caret position is never passed automatically. Tools that need position information must accept explicit parameters:

  • line: Int (1-based line number)
  • column: Int (1-based column number)

items.title: Converting Line/Column to Offset
items.text:
import com.intellij.openapi.fileEditor.FileDocumentManager
import com.intellij.psi.PsiDocumentManager
import com.intellij.util.DocumentUtil

suspend fun work_with_position(
    filePath: String,
    line: Int,
    column: Int
) {
    val project = currentCoroutineContext().project
    val virtualFile = LocalFileSystem.getInstance().findFileByNioFile(resolvedPath)
        ?: mcpFail("File not found: $filePath")

    readAction {
        val document = FileDocumentManager.getInstance().getDocument(virtualFile)
            ?: mcpFail("Cannot read file: $filePath")

        // Validate line (0-based internally)
        if (!DocumentUtil.isValidLine(line - 1, document)) {
            mcpFail("Line number is out of bounds")
        }

        // Convert to offset
        val lineStartOffset = document.getLineStartOffset(line - 1)
        val offset = lineStartOffset + column - 1

        // Validate offset
        if (!DocumentUtil.isValidOffset(offset, document)) {
            mcpFail("Line and column $line:$column (offset=$offset) is out of bounds")
        }

        // Use offset to find PSI elements
        val psiFile = PsiDocumentManager.getInstance(project).getPsiFile(document)
        val psiReference = psiFile?.findReferenceAt(offset)
        val element = psiReference?.resolve()
    }
}

items.title: Example from CodeInsightToolset
items.text:
@McpTool
suspend fun get_symbol_info(
    @McpDescription("Relative path to file from project root")
    filePath: String,
    @McpDescription("1-based line number")
    line: Int,
    @McpDescription("1-based column number")
    column: Int,
): SymbolInfoResult {
    val project = currentCoroutineContext().project
    val resolvedPath = project.resolveInProject(filePath)
    val virtualFile = LocalFileSystem.getInstance().refreshAndFindFileByNioFile(resolvedPath)
        ?: mcpFail("File not found: $filePath")

    val (documentationTargets, symbolInfo) = readAction {
        val document = FileDocumentManager.getInstance().getDocument(virtualFile)
            ?: mcpFail("Cannot read file: $filePath")
        val psiFile = PsiDocumentManager.getInstance(project).getPsiFile(document)
            ?: mcpFail("Cannot get symbol information for file '$filePath'")

        if (!DocumentUtil.isValidLine(line - 1, document)) {
            mcpFail("Line number is out of bounds of the document")
        }

        val lineStartOffset = document.getLineStartOffset(line - 1)
        val offset = lineStartOffset + column - 1

        if (!DocumentUtil.isValidOffset(offset, document)) {
            mcpFail("Line and column $line:$column(offset=$offset) is out of bounds")
        }

        val psiReference = psiFile.findReferenceAt(offset)
        val resolvedReference = psiReference?.resolve()

        documentationTargets(psiFile, offset).map { it.createPointer() } to 
            resolvedReference?.let { getElementSymbolInfo(it, extraLines = 1) }
    }

    // ... rest of implementation
}

items.title: Opening Files in Editor
items.text:
Use FileEditorManagerEx.openFile() to open files:

import com.intellij.openapi.application.EDT
import com.intellij.openapi.fileEditor.ex.FileEditorManagerEx
import com.intellij.openapi.fileEditor.impl.FileEditorOpenOptions
import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers
import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext

suspend fun open_file(filePath: String) {
    val project = currentCoroutineContext().project
    val resolvedPath = project.resolveInProject(filePath)

    val file = LocalFileSystem.getInstance().findFileByNioFile(resolvedPath)
        ?: LocalFileSystem.getInstance().refreshAndFindFileByNioFile(resolvedPath)
        ?: mcpFail("File not found: $filePath")

    // Must be called on EDT (Event Dispatch Thread)
    withContext(Dispatchers.EDT) {
        FileEditorManagerEx.getInstanceExAsync(project)
            .openFile(file, options = FileEditorOpenOptions(requestFocus = true))
    }
}

items.title: Example from FileToolset
items.text:
@McpTool
@McpDescription("""
    Opens the specified file in the JetBrains IDE editor.
    The file path can be absolute or relative to the project root.
""")
suspend fun open_file_in_editor(
    @McpDescription("Relative path to file from project root")
    filePath: String,
) {
    currentCoroutineContext().reportToolActivity(
        McpServerBundle.message("tool.activity.opening.file", filePath)
    )
    val project = currentCoroutineContext().project
    val resolvedPath = project.resolveInProject(filePath)

    val file = LocalFileSystem.getInstance().findFileByNioFile(resolvedPath)
        ?: LocalFileSystem.getInstance().refreshAndFindFileByNioFile(resolvedPath)

    if (file == null || !file.exists() || !file.isFile) {
        mcpFail("File $filePath doesn't exist or can't be opened")
    }

    withContext(Dispatchers.EDT) {
        FileEditorManagerEx.getInstanceExAsync(project)
            .openFile(file, options = FileEditorOpenOptions(requestFocus = true))
    }
}

items.title: Navigation to Specific Position
items.text:
While not directly exposed in current MCP toolsets, you can navigate to a specific position using OpenFileDescriptor:

import com.intellij.openapi.fileEditor.OpenFileDescriptor
import com.intellij.openapi.application.EDT
import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers
import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext

suspend fun navigate_to_position(
    filePath: String,
    line: Int,
    column: Int
) {
    val project = currentCoroutineContext().project
    val virtualFile = LocalFileSystem.getInstance().findFileByNioFile(resolvedPath)
        ?: mcpFail("File not found: $filePath")

    withContext(Dispatchers.EDT) {
        // OpenFileDescriptor uses 0-based line and column
        val descriptor = OpenFileDescriptor(project, virtualFile, line - 1, column - 1)
        descriptor.navigate(true) // true = request focus
    }
}

items.title: 5. Available Context from CoroutineContext
items.text:
From McpCallInfo.kt, the following context is available:

// Project context
val project: Project = currentCoroutineContext().project
val projectOrNull: Project? = currentCoroutineContext().projectOrNull

// Client information
val clientInfo: ClientInfo = currentCoroutineContext().clientInfo
// Contains: name, version

// Tool descriptor
val toolDescriptor: McpToolDescriptor = currentCoroutineContext().currentToolDescriptor

// Full call info
val callInfo: McpCallInfo = currentCoroutineContext().mcpCallInfo
// Contains: callId, clientInfo, project, mcpToolDescriptor, rawArguments, meta, 
//           mcpSessionOptions, headers

items.text:
@McpTool
suspend fun my_file_tool(
    @McpDescription("Relative path to file from project root")

): String {
    val project = currentCoroutineContext().project

        ?: LocalFileSystem.getInstance().refreshAndFindFileByNioFile(resolvedPath)

        val document = FileDocumentManager.getInstance().getDocument(virtualFile)

        val psiFile = PsiDocumentManager.getInstance(project).getPsiFile(document)
            ?: mcpFail("Cannot get PSI file: $pathInProject")

        "Success"

}

items.text:

    @McpDescription("1-based line number")

    return readAction {

items.title: Pattern 3: Editor Manipulation Tool
items.text:
@McpTool
suspend fun my_editor_tool(
    @McpDescription("Relative path to file from project root")
    pathInProject: String
): String {
    val project = currentCoroutineContext().project
    val resolvedPath = project.resolveInProject(pathInProject)

    val virtualFile = LocalFileSystem.getInstance().findFileByNioFile(resolvedPath)
        ?: mcpFail("File not found: $pathInProject")

    // Open file in editor
    withContext(Dispatchers.EDT) {
        FileEditorManagerEx.getInstanceExAsync(project)
            .openFile(virtualFile, options = FileEditorOpenOptions(requestFocus = true))
    }

    return "File opened successfully"
}

items.title: 7. Key Takeaways
items.text:
1. Project context is automatically available via currentCoroutineContext().project
  2. Editor context is NOT automatic - use FileEditorManagerEx to access editors
  3. Caret position is NOT automatic - accept line and column as explicit parameters
  4. Navigation is done via FileEditorManagerEx.openFile() or OpenFileDescriptor.navigate()
  5. File paths should be relative to project root and passed as parameters
  6. Position parameters should be 1-based (line and column) for user-friendliness
  7. Offset calculations are 0-based internally (convert from 1-based parameters)
  8. EDT thread is required for UI operations like opening files
  9. Read actions are required for PSI operations
  10. Write actions are required for modifying files

items.title: Settings
items.text: The Python BetterPy plugin is highly configurable. You can find its settings under: Settings/Preferences > Languages & Frameworks > Python BetterPy.

items.title: Feature Toggles
items.text: Almost every intention, inspection, and action can be enabled or disabled individually. This allows you to tailor the plugin to your specific workflow and avoid clutter if you don't use certain features.

items.title: Type Wrapping Settings
items.text:
• Prefer project types: When wrapping a value that could match multiple types (e.g., in a Union), should the plugin prioritize types defined in your project over standard library types?
  • Include stdlib types: Should standard library types (like Path) be suggested as wrapping candidates?

items.title: Parameter Object Settings
items.text:
• Default base type: Choose the default class type used when creating a new Parameter Object. Options typically include:
    • dataclass (Default)
    • pydantic.BaseModel
    • NamedTuple
    • TypedDict

items.title: Import Settings
items.text:
• Use relative imports: Toggle the preference for relative imports when the plugin generates new code or performs refactorings.
  • Restore source root prefix: Control whether the plugin should attempt to preserve/restore source root prefixes in import paths.

items.title: Actions
items.text: Beyond intentions and inspections, the plugin provides several global and context-specific actions.

items.title: Copy Special Menu
items.text:
Found under Edit > Copy Special or in context menus.

  • BetterPy: Copy with Dependencies: Copies selected code along with its local dependencies and imports.
  • Copy Package Content: Copies the content of an entire Python package.
  • Copy Build Number: Copies the current IDE build number (useful for bug reports).
  • Copy Fully Qualified Names (FQN): Copies the full import path of the selected symbol(s).

items.title: Pytest Tree Actions
items.text:
Available when right-clicking nodes in the Pytest results tool window.

  • Copy Pytest Node IDs: Useful for running specific tests from the command line.
  • Copy Stacktrace: Provides a cleaned-up version of the failure stacktrace.
  • Toggle Pytest Skip: Skips or unskips the selected test(s).

items.title: Navigation Actions
items.text: • Jump to Pytest Node: Navigates from a test function in the editor to its result in the test tree.

items.title: Console & Usage Filtering
items.text: Tools to reduce noise and improve focus during development and debugging.

items.title: Console Filter
items.text: The Py Message Console Filter automatically processes output in the Python console and execution tool windows. It can highlight or hide specific patterns, making it easier to spot relevant information in verbose logs.

items.title: Usage Filtering Rules
items.text: The plugin introduces custom rules for the Find Usages (Alt+F7) functionality.

items.title: Type Annotation Usage Filtering
items.text: Allows you to filter out usages that only occur within type annotations. This is extremely useful when you want to find where a class is actually instantiated or called, rather than just where its name is used as a type hint.

items.title: Import Handling
items.text: The plugin provides advanced features for managing Python imports, especially useful in large DDD projects with complex folder structures.

items.title: Relative vs Absolute Imports
items.text: The plugin can be configured to prefer relative imports when moving code or performing refactorings within the same package.

items.title: Restore Source Root Prefix
items.text: When copying FQNs or performing refactorings, the plugin can automatically handle source root prefixes to ensure that imports remain valid regardless of how your IDE is configured (e.g., whether the src folder is marked as a source root).

items.title: Export Symbol to Target
items.text: This feature helps you move a symbol and update its imports, or "export" it through a public API module (like __init__.py).

items.title: File-Based vs Stub-Based Indices in IntelliJ Platform
items.text: This document explains the two main indexing mechanisms available in the IntelliJ Platform, and why PyLambdaFileIndex correctly uses a file-based index rather than a stub-based one.
path: File-Based vs Stub-Based Indices in IntelliJ Platform

items.title: The Two Indexing Mechanisms
path: File-Based vs Stub-Based Indices in IntelliJ Platform

items.title: File-Based Indices (FileBasedIndexExtension)
items.text:
A file-based index operates directly on raw file content. The platform feeds each file's bytes (and optionally its PSI tree) to a DataIndexer, which produces a map of keys → values. The index is stored on disk and queried via FileBasedIndex.getInstance().

Key characteristics:

  • Input: raw FileContent (bytes + lazily-built PSI). The indexer receives a FileContent object and can call inputData.psiFile to get the PSI tree.
  • Scope: any file type — source files, library JARs, .class files, .xml, etc.
  • Query API: FileBasedIndex.getContainingFiles(name, key, scope), getValues(...), getAllKeys(...).
  • Rebuild trigger: the file's content changes (timestamp/hash).
  • Base class: ScalarIndexExtension<K> (keys only, no values) or FileBasedIndexExtension<K, V>.
path: File-Based vs Stub-Based Indices in IntelliJ Platform

items.title: Stub-Based Indices (StubIndexExtension)
items.text:
A stub index operates on the stub tree — a lightweight, serialisable skeleton of the PSI tree that captures only the declarations (classes, functions, fields, top-level assignments, etc.) without method bodies or expressions.

Key characteristics:

  • Input: a StubElement tree produced by the language's IStubFileElementType / StubElementType. The stub tree is built once and cached separately from the full PSI.
  • Scope: only files whose language has a stub-producing element type. For Python this means .py files processed by PyFileElementType.
  • Query API: StubIndex.getInstance().get(key, name, project, scope) — returns PSI elements directly (e.g. PyFunction, PyClass).
  • Rebuild trigger: the stub tree changes (i.e. the file's declarations change).
  • Base class: StringStubIndexExtension<Psi> or StubIndexExtension<K, Psi>.
  • Populated via: indexStub(stub, sink) on a StubElementType, or via a CustomTargetExpressionStubType extension point (see fixture-stub-index.md).
path: File-Based vs Stub-Based Indices in IntelliJ Platform

items.title: When to Use Each
items.text:
Criterion File-Based Index Stub-Based Index What you need to find Files (or arbitrary data) Named declarations (classes, functions, …) Data lives in Expressions, bodies, any syntax Top-level / class-level declarations only Language requirement Any file type Language must produce stubs Query returns VirtualFile or raw values PSI elements Typical use case "Which files contain X?" "Give me the PyFunction named foo"

Rule of thumb: use a stub index when you are indexing named declarations that appear in the stub tree. Use a file-based index when you need to record a fact about a file as a whole, or when the data you care about lives inside expressions or function bodies (which are not part of the stub tree).
path: File-Based vs Stub-Based Indices in IntelliJ Platform

items.title: Why PyLambdaFileIndex Must Be File-Based
items.text:
PyLambdaFileIndex (in core/index/PyLambdaFileIndex.kt) answers the question:

"Which Python source files contain at least one lambda expression?"

There are two concrete reasons why a stub-based index cannot answer this question.
path: File-Based vs Stub-Based Indices in IntelliJ Platform

items.title: 1. Lambda expressions are not part of the stub tree
items.text:
The Python stub tree captures declarations: PyFunction, PyClass, PyTargetExpression at module/class scope, etc. A PyLambdaExpression is an expression — it can appear inside a function body, a default argument, a list comprehension, or any other expression context. Expression nodes are deliberately excluded from stubs to keep them small and fast.

Because PyLambdaExpression nodes are never present in the stub tree, a StubElementType for them cannot be registered, and indexStub() would never be called for them. A stub index simply has no access to this data.
path: File-Based vs Stub-Based Indices in IntelliJ Platform

items.title: 2. The index records a file-level fact, not a named declaration
items.text:
PyLambdaFileIndex stores a single marker key ("lambda") per file — it is a boolean "this file has lambdas" flag. Stub indices are designed to map names to PSI elements (e.g. function name → PyFunction). There is no named declaration to return here; the caller only needs the VirtualFile to open it and inspect it further.

The query call in the companion object reflects this exactly:

// PyLambdaFileIndex.kt
fun findFilesWithLambdas(project: Project, scope: GlobalSearchScope): Collection<VirtualFile> {
    return FileBasedIndex.getInstance().getContainingFiles(NAME, LAMBDA_MARKER, scope)
}

getContainingFiles is a FileBasedIndex API — there is no equivalent on StubIndex because stub queries return PSI elements, not files.
path: File-Based vs Stub-Based Indices in IntelliJ Platform

items.title: 3. The indexer uses the full PSI tree
items.text:
The indexer calls PsiTreeUtil.findChildOfType(psiFile, PyLambdaExpression::class.java), which walks the complete PSI tree including all expression nodes. This is only possible in a DataIndexer that receives a FileContent object with a lazily-built full PSI tree. A stub-based indexer only ever sees the stub tree, which, as noted above, contains no PyLambdaExpression nodes.

// PyLambdaFileIndex.kt — indexer body
override fun getIndexer(): DataIndexer<String, Void, FileContent> {
    return DataIndexer { inputData ->
        val result = mutableMapOf<String, Void?>()
        if (inputData.fileType == PythonFileType.INSTANCE) {
            val psiFile = inputData.psiFile as? PyFile ?: return@DataIndexer result
            // PsiTreeUtil walks the FULL PSI tree — not available in stub indexers
            val hasLambda = PsiTreeUtil.findChildOfType(psiFile, PyLambdaExpression::class.java) != null
            if (hasLambda) result[LAMBDA_MARKER] = null
        }
        result
    }
}
path: File-Based vs Stub-Based Indices in IntelliJ Platform

items.title: Contrast: When a Stub Index Would Be Correct
items.text:
For comparison, consider fixture-stub-index.md, which describes indexing assigned fixtures of the form x = pytest.fixture()(func). That case is a good fit for a stub index because:

  • The indexed node is a PyTargetExpression — a top-level assignment, which is part of the stub tree.
  • The query returns a named PSI element (PyTargetExpression for fixture name x).
  • The CustomTargetExpressionStubType extension point already hooks into stub building for exactly this pattern.

PyLambdaFileIndex is the opposite: the data lives in expressions (not declarations), the result is a file (not a PSI element), and the detection requires a full-PSI walk. A file-based index is therefore not just acceptable — it is the only correct choice.
path: File-Based vs Stub-Based Indices in IntelliJ Platform

items.title: Refactoring & Code Transformations
items.text: BetterPy provides 5 refactoring intentions and actions — from populating function arguments to extracting protocols and converting between code patterns.

items.title: Make parameter optional
items.text:
Since 2026.04.05 · Maturity Incubating

Converts a required parameter to an optional one by adding a default value.

How to invoke: Alt+Enter → "BetterPy: Make optional"

BeforeAfter 
def greet(name: str, title: str):
    pass

def greet(name: str, title: str = ""):
    pass

items.title: Make parameter mandatory
items.text:
Since 2026.04.05 · Maturity Incubating

Converts an optional parameter to a required one by removing the default value.

How to invoke: Alt+Enter → "BetterPy: Make mandatory"

BeforeAfter 
def greet(name: str, title: str = ""):
    pass

def greet(name: str, title: str):
    pass

items.title: Parameter object refactoring
items.text: Since 2026.04.05 · Maturity Incubating · Issues PY-59270

items.title: Introduce Parameter Object
items.text:
Groups multiple function parameters into a single dataclass.

How to invoke: Refactor menu → "BetterPy: Introduce Parameter Object…"

BeforeAfter 
def create_order(customer_id: int, product: str, quantity: int, price: float):
    pass

@dataclass
class CreateOrderParams:
    customer_id: int
    product: str
    quantity: int
    price: float

def create_order(params: CreateOrderParams):
    pass

items.title: Inline Parameter Object
items.text:
The inverse of Introduce — inlines a parameter object back into individual parameters.

How to invoke: Refactor menu → "BetterPy: Inline Parameter Object…"

items.title: Copy method annotations from parent
Typing & Type Hints
items.text: BetterPy enhances PyCharm's type system support with smart wrapping/unwrapping intentions, completions driven by expected types, and convenient annotation editing tools.

items.title: NewType/TypeVar/ParamSpec reference & rename
items.text:
Since 2026.04.05 · Maturity Stable · Issues PY-82966

Adds reference support for NewType, TypeVar, and ParamSpec name string literals, enabling navigation from the string to its usage sites. Renaming the variable also updates the name string literal automatically.

How to invoke:

  • Ctrl + click on the name string in a NewType("UserId", int) call to navigate.
  • Shift+F6 on the definition to rename — the string literal stays in sync.
BeforeAfter 
UserId = NewType("UserId", int)

AccountId = NewType("AccountId", int)

items.title: Strip signature type annotations
items.text:

def create_user(name, email, age):
    pass

items.text:
1. Open Settings → Plugins → Marketplace.

  2. Open Settings → Plugins → → Install Plugin from Disk…
  3. Select the downloaded .zip file and restart the IDE.

items.title: First-Use Orientation
items.text: After installation, BetterPy is ready to go with sensible defaults.

items.title: Status Bar Widget
items.text: Look for the BetterPy widget in the bottom status bar. It shows the plugin status and provides quick access to settings.

items.title: Settings Panel
items.text:
Open Settings → Tools → BetterPy to see all feature toggles organized by group:

  • Typing & Type Hints
  • Refactoring & Code Transformations

Each feature can be individually enabled or disabled. Incubating features are marked with .

items.title: Your First Intention: Make Parameter Optional
items.text:
Try BetterPy right away with the Make Parameter Optional intention:

BeforeAfter 
def create_user(name: str, email: str, age: int):
    pass
# Place caret on `age` parameter

def create_user(name: str, email: str, age: int | None = None):
    pass

How to invoke: Place the caret on a required parameter and press Alt+Enter, then select "BetterPy: Make optional".

Tip

Make Parameter Optional adds a default value to the selected parameter. Use the complementary Make Parameter Mandatory intention to remove a default value.

items.title: Inspections
items.text: The plugin provides several inspections to ensure code quality and adherence to DDD principles.

items.title: Missing Dataclass Decorator
items.text: Warns when a class appears to be used as a Value Object (e.g., it's a subclass of another Value Object or used in wrapping intentions) but is missing the @dataclass decorator.

items.title: Missing Symbol in __all__
items.text: Warns when a public symbol (class, function, or variable) is defined in a module but not included in its __all__ list. Includes a quick-fix to add the symbol to __all__.

items.title: Private Module Import
items.text: Warns when you import symbols from a "private" module (one whose name starts with an underscore). DDD encourages importing through public APIs.

items.title: Shadowing Stdlib Module
items.text: Warns when a project module has the same name as a standard library module, which can lead to confusing import errors.

items.title: Constant is not Final
items.text: Warns when a variable that looks like a constant (uppercase naming) is not annotated with Final.

items.title: Abstract Method Not Implemented
items.text: Ensures all abstract methods are implemented in concrete subclasses.
